CONTENTS ARTICLES Boundaries and Roles in Ministry Counseling 1 Miriam Stark Parent, PhD As we move into the 21st century church and ministry related counseling struggle to identify the boundaries of good risk management and compassionate caregiving. Clergy are no longer safe from litigation for failure to adequately care for those they serve. In many ways, pastoral and ministry related counseling demand even more awareness of boundaries than secular professional settings. Common boundary is- sues involve multiple role relationships; sexuality issues pertaining to gender and age; information and confidentiality demands; and issues of counseling competency. This article discusses each of these issues and articulates some of the ethical and le- gal concerns surrounding each issue. KEYWORDS. All rights reserved. doi:10.1300/J062v08n02_01 1 In Matthew 10 Jesus is preparing his twelve closest followers for a preaching and healing ministry. He gives them power and authority to drive out demons and to cure diseases. He sends them out to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick. Carefully he instructs them, warn- ing them of dangers and difficulties while encouraging them in their ministry purpose. Included in that passage is a succinct statement where Jesus sums up the situation and offers a metaphor for their conduct. He says: “I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves” (Mt 10:16 NIV). In Jewish lore the snake was often an emblem of cunning, while the dove was seen as simple, even stupid. However, in combination each corrects the weakness of the other, balancing prudence or wisdom in the face of dan- ger with a disarming, even harmless, innocence in escaping it (Jamie- son, Fausset, & Brown, 1945). In the same way, Paul urges the believers at Rome to be “wise about what is good, and innocent about what is evil” (Ro 16:19). Wisdom and innocence were to walk hand-in-hand in guiding their conduct. As it was true for the disciples in Jesus’ day, it is true today. There are dangers and difficulties in the ministry of healing to which those in- volved in pastoral and counseling ministries aspire. There are indeed “wolves” circling, waiting to attack at the first sign of weakness or vul- nerability. Those who serve Jesus openly and proclaim his message clearly, will encounter practical, relational and spiritual dangers. While awareness and wise behavior can decrease vulnerability, the only real defense comes as we allow the Holy Spirit to work in us, as well as through us. CHANGING RULES Dealing with 21st Century Ambiguities In North America the retrospective clarity and simplicity of the 20th century has given way to the constantly changing, nanosecond technol- ogy of the 21st century. Even as the Industrial Revolution brought about major societal changes, so the Technological Revolution, compounded by population mobility and increased awareness of multicultural dy- namics, among other social trends, is changing the face of counseling ministries inside and outside the church. For those involved in serving communities of faith, the dangers and dilemmas have increased significantly. For years much was overlooked 2 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING or forgiven on the basis of good intent. Innocence was presumed. To- day, the church is no longer so naive or forgiving. The recent scandals in the Roman Catholic church have only served to highlight some of the problems. Lawsuits against spiritual leaders who appear to have abused their privileged position are now expected and anticipated, rather than unthinkable. Society has become cynical and jaded in its expectations of leadership, whether it is in the White House or the pulpit. It is no longer unthinkable to bring suit against public, professional or spiritual fig- ures. The presumption of good intent when evaluating public actions has faded and been replaced by a certain amount of skepticism. Church-Related Counseling The 1960s and 70s saw the migration of professional counseling into the Christian church. Large churches and small were interested in hiring professionally trained counselors or affiliating with specific practices. Professional licensure or certification was seen as a way to enhance ser- vice and decrease liability. That was followed by substantial backlash in the 1980s and 90s. For some this was partly ideologically driven by theological concerns. However, one of the more compelling practical concerns was the rise of malpractice litigation in the mental health field and the substantial liability incurred by churches offering counseling services. Severing ties with professional counseling, however, failed to stem the tide of church and clergy-related suits. In keeping with the present cul- tural ethos, churches and their insurers are perceived as “deep pockets” from which large sums might be extracted. Although the church ulti- mately prevailed, the case of Nally vs. Grace Community Church in- volved Rev. John MacArthur’s church in legal action for years and set precedents that have significantly impacted counseling ministry prac- tices. As we move into the 21st century church-related counseling is again on the rise. However, it is taking many forms. While fewer churches run full-scale professional counseling practices, many churches have begun to make arrangements with trusted independent therapists to offer ser- vices for church members or to use church facilities. Others have em- phasized lay or peer counseling ministries, such as Stephen Ministries. Many have preferred bringing on pastoral or ministry staff to do pasto- ral counseling under the direct auspices of the church. Consequently, the struggle to find an appropriate balance between in- stitutional risk management and compassionate caregiving continues. Miriam Stark Parent 3 While such terms are not mutually exclusive, often a lack of education and discernment, coupled with legitimate fear and frustration, can make them feel like they are. Yet, despite the increasing risks, God continues to call Christians to a ministry of counseling and healing. It therefore becomes crucial to understand the legal, professional and social param- eters that lead to wise practice. Wisdom in practice and innocence in character can be a powerful combination: reinforcing each other and synergistically strengthening ministry. Law and Ethics Governmental law represents the minimum standard that a society sets on the behavior of its citizens. It is generally reactive and punitive: policing society’s interactions and relationships. United States legal tra- dition and, more specifically, the United States Constitution, have gen- erally exempted churches and clergy from liability for negligent or improper actions based on the First Amendment doctrine of religious freedom. Even today clergy malpractice is rarely successfully prose- cuted. The cases that are justified are usually against pastors or counsel- ors who intentionally commit harm. These are often the result of acts of seduction, child abuse, and defamation of character (Levicoff, 1991). Given society’s concern about victims, personal rights, and abuse of power, it is likely that suits against institutions that have traditionally held power will continue to proliferate. The first clergy misconduct suits appeared in 1984, and the numbers grew dramatically before level- ing off somewhat in the mid 1990s (Christian Century, 1998). While some of these have failed for good reasons, far too many have rightly prevailed. Such justified lawsuits hurt the reputation of others and cause a domino effect in suits brought to court. In addition, the emotional damage is often compounded by a bitter sense of spiritual betrayal which demands that the church, and those as- sociated with her, be held to a higher standard than secular law. As leader after leader has publically admitted to personal moral lapses, the suspicion with which counselors and ministry leaders are viewed has deepened. Professional misconduct involving sexuality, child abuse or insurance fraud, has also become fertile ground for lawsuits against religious practitioners. For those whose primary focus in ministry is professional counseling, there are organizational ethics codes (e.g., American Counseling Associ- ation Code of Ethics) which spell out the professional responsibilities of the practitioner. These become the basis for understanding the standard of 4 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING care that the law requires. For the professional counselor attention to the appropriate ethics code is essential. However, clergy often have no clear code of ethics which clarifies their responsibilities, leaving action open to a personal, denominational, or local interpretation of God’s expectations. Often counselors working in faith community settings are unaware or un- concerned about the various ethics codes. This is a dangerous situation. Ethics codes are not only binding on members; the legal system relies on them to define professional standard of care. While the duty of care has not been well defined for non-licensed counselors in ministry settings, it may well be implied. One author has noted: “To the extent that pastoral counseling activities parallel those of a secular professional counselor, society will hold that pastoral counselor to the same standards regarding ethics and quality of care as established for the professional” (Berman, 1997, 268). Although clergy are generally free from common-law liability for negligent counseling (Young and Griffith, 1999), pastoral counselors and those offering counseling service under the auspices of the church may not assume they have the same religious freedom protection. “While no states have, to date, recognized clergy malpractice claims, courts are increasingly accepting suits based on a breach of fiduciary duty or complaints of intentional infliction of emotional distress. These types of claims are more likely to result from incongruent expectations and resulting frustrations over counseling interventions and outcomes, as well as sexual misconduct” (Hagglund & Weimer, 2000). Although we may find such intrusion threatening and constraining, Scripture reminds us that we are to submit to the governing authorities God has placed over us, “not only because of possible punishment but also because of conscience” (Ro 13:5b). The balance between church and state responsibility must be carefully played out in our lives and in our counseling ministries. Wise and godly practice, therefore, demands a knowledge of the appropriate state and federal laws, as well as an un- derstanding of the appropriate ethical codes and standards of practice. Such knowledge and wisdom must be built into those personal bound- aries by which we live our personal and professional lives. Boundaries or Rules Just as there are boundaries to define the limits of a parcel of land, there are human boundaries which define personal limits. Those indi- vidual parameters or boundaries define and give substance to our hu- man relationships. They are inextricably intertwined with how we Miriam Stark Parent 5 define the roles that govern our interactions. Boundaries support rela- tionships and give structure within which relationships can grow. They allow us to determine what we are responsible for in a relationship and the appropriate limits of that relationship. Numerous books have been written (e.g., Cloud & Townsend, 1992) to help us set healthy bound- aries based on biblical principles of relationship and service, rather than self interest. Our personal boundaries are often conveyed nonverbally as well as verbally and may be determined by personal worldview, by role, by cus- tom and even by law. They are present in every relationship we have, but differ in intensity and practice according to the nature of the rela- tionship. In most helping relationships, boundaries are maintained pri- marily for the benefit of the counselee, who is often vulnerable and in need. In counseling, boundaries are designed to provide relationships with structure and safety. “ . . . Boundaries provide structure for the process, safety for the client, and the required emotional distance for effective therapeutic work” (Welfel, 2002, 155). They also become the means by which we manage both power and vulnerability in relationships. There is a relative balance of power that is present in every relationship and boundaries help negotiate those issues to prevent doing harm to the vul- nerable. For example, healthy families set implicit, and sometimes ex- plicit, boundaries on discipline practices. These are designed to prevent the stronger adult from inflicting abuse on other emotionally and physi- cally vulnerable family members. The limits and parameters of those boundaries may, of course, vary significantly by family and by culture. Just as professional parameters encapsulated in ethics codes include societal laws, so our personal boundaries ought to reflect attention to professional ethics and the laws of the region where we practice. Where societal and professional ethics and law are consistent with Christian principles, we need to draw them into our daily practice. Where they are in conflict with God’s clear expectations and calling, we need to stand firm, accepting the reality of human consequences for such civil disobe- dience. Such things are, of course, easy to say and much harder to live. Every individual, every situation and every interaction brings with it a unique and complex set of decisions and choices. Given the complexity of human interactions, it often seems easier to establish a set of behav- ioral rules, rather than to try to articulate permeable boundaries to serve as guidelines. The word boundary merely denotes a line or marker that indicates a limit. In contrast, the word rule implies a power and authority behind a 6 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING prohibition of some type. Someone with the power and authority to do so, has likely mandated a rule which is then imposed on those with less au- thority. This is not necessarily a bad thing as organizations and relation- ships respond to structure. If the rules are set thoughtfully and carefully for those with less discernment, they can be beneficial. However, as soci- ety becomes more and more secular, as well as litigious, those in counsel- ing ministries can find themselves hiding behind self-protective rules and inhibitory regulations that minimize personal responsibility in favor of corporate obedience. Because a rule is imposed, whether on self or oth- ers, once it is crossed, it must either be forever expanded to cover the ex- cursion or considered broken with punitive penalties implied. Conversely, boundaries act more as rubber bands. They can be ex- panded under significant pressure, but are designed to return immedi- ately to their original shape when the pressure is released. Boundaries in counseling relationships need to be flexible, not losing their shape, but capable of expanding when necessary. Such expansion, however, need not dictate a new boundary. Expansion ought to create significant pres- sure to return the boundary to its normal parameter. To continue the analogy further, even a rubber band has limits beyond which it cannot expand without snapping. It is important to recognize that our counsel- ing boundaries also have such limits. When the pressure on the bound- ary becomes too great, the relationship is at risk. Therefore, it is critical to understand the difference between an appropriate boundary crossing or extension and a clear boundary violation, which jeopardizes the entire structure of the relationship. ...a boundary crossing is a departure from common practice with the intent to benefit a client and with some credible evidence that benefit is likely to result. ...A boundary violation or boundary break is a departure from accepted practice that causes the client harm or is very likely to cause harm. Implicit in this definition is the notion that the harm probably could (and should) have been an- ticipated if the professional either had more altruistic intent or was more rigorous in analyzing the risks and merits of the action before it was undertaken. (Welfel, 2002, 156) If we are to be both wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil (Ro 16:19), we are going to have to be much more intentional in recognizing and setting our boundaries and dealing with the variety of issues that emerge from them. Among the many issues that arise in Miriam Stark Parent 7 counseling ministries, four broad areas account for the majority of con- cern and questions. FOUR COMMON BOUNDARY ISSUES Multiple Roles In real life all of us carry multiple roles. We are many things simul- taneously, often to the same person. If we are able to clearly define and hold the appropriate role boundaries and the other person recognizes, accepts and respects those boundaries, all works well. However, when various role boundaries become confused or are not clearly explained, the potential for misunderstanding and damaged relationships is great. This is especially critical in counseling where boundaries create the safety and structure necessary to a ministry of healing. For many years psychoanalytic theory subtly dictated the placement and emphasis on therapeutic boundaries in secular mental health rela- tionships. In addition understanding the imbalance of power inherent in the counseling relationship and the human tendency to misuse that power mandated the development of explicit limits. From their incep- tion the various mental health professions incorporated what they felt were some basic safeguards into the professional ethics codes. The ap- plication of those legitimate concerns was easily converted into a uni- versal ban on any other role relationship once a counseling relationship was established. That worked very well for many years when counsel- ing primarily involved a secular, urban, increasingly mobile and gener- ally western/European population who responded to that kind of anonymity and life compartmentalization. In pastoral counseling, various ethnic communities, and many ru- ral settings, this kind of practice was never possible. Pastors, by vir- tue of their position, have always struggled with multiple roles, especially when they counsel. They frequently function as friend, teacher, spiritual advisor, shepherd, and sometimes even coworker. In many rural or ethnic communities counseling can only be done when a long term social relationship has been established that builds the necessary trust and expectations, so that assistance can be re- quested. 8 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING Boundary Confusion Every role brings with it unique obligations and expectations. When those roles differ significantly, the risk of harm to the less powerful, more vulnerable individual is increased. In addition the responsibilities inherent in differing roles may create divided loyalties and expecta- tions. A financially strapped pastor, counseling a member of the elder board which determines pastoral salaries, may find objectivity difficult. Yet a certain measure of objectivity is implied in the counseling role. Even more than in secular settings, counselees are vulnerable when they consult counselors in church settings. Counselees often have exag- gerated expectations of the safety and ethical considerations in church- based counseling due to the spiritual emphasis and ministerial back- ground of the counselor. Therefore, they may grant them extraordinary trust, power and authority or desire special closeness and attention (Haug, 1999). The church has often struggled with issues of power and authority. Counseling ministers often have an ambivalent attitude toward issues of power and authority, preferring to consider the relationship one of friend- ship (Haug, 1999). Because of this they tend to minimize their influence and, therefore, their responsibility for the relationship. It is comforting to believe that we have less power and influence over people’s lives than is sometimes true. As congregations and ministries become more ethnically and racially diverse, we must recognize that normative Euro-American boundaries may need adapting. Other cultures may not place the same value on in- dividualism and anonymity. Likewise authority, especially spiritual au- thority, may be viewed very differently depending on cultural world- view. Being a known and respected elder in the church may be a benefit in one setting and preclude any kind of openness in another. With in- creasing cultural diversity in many ministries, the counselor may find him or herself in the same role with totally different expectations and boundaries from one relationship to the next. Negotiating those differ- ences requires increased awareness, cultural skills and much wisdom. Policy Statements It becomes obvious then that there need to be clearly defined bound- aries and responsibilities in ministry counseling relationships. In profes- sional settings some boundaries are universally acknowledged and may be implicitly assumed. In ministry settings, such things can rarely be taken for granted. Hence the need for consistent policies intended to mini- Miriam Stark Parent 9 mize the differences in expectations between counselor and counselee. The use of clearly written and articulated policy statements has acquired an urgency previously lacking in ministry-related counseling. Clearly stated policies regarding the types of counseling offered (e.g., peer, pastoral, professional, etc.), the duration of counseling (e.g., three sessions only), place and space, financial arrangements, and coun- selor availability provide crucial boundaries that provide structure and limit the potential for differing expectations. Without the open discus- sion of such policies, boundary crossings are hard to regulate and easily become boundary violations. Differing expectations about the use of time, social relationships and confidentiality limits, among other prac- tices become a “slippery slope” from which harm and loss of ministry often emerge. Sunday morning church-aisle-counseling not only violates confidenti- ality and safety concerns, but frequently destroys the possibility of genu- ine worship for the counselor, whose greatest concern in the service becomes how close to the door to sit! Yet it can seem logical to the counselee to use that time to fill the counselor in on the critical events of the weekend. Without explicit discussion such settings become fertile soil for hurt feelings and misunderstandings that limit effective ministry. While multiple roles are a fact of life in many settings, the counselor must be aware that it is his or her responsibility, not the counselee’s, to clearly define and set the boundaries of each relationship and to be will- ing to redefine them as roles change. When roles or responsibilities con- flict, supervision and/or consultation is expected and indispensable if counseling is to be productive. Open discussion with counselees con- cerning expectations, possible role conflicts and counseling boundaries must become a norm in our ministry settings. Written informed consent procedures can be of great assistance in preventing role conflicts or un- certainties. Good informed consent policies should cover the practical- ities of counseling services, such as time and place limitations, as well as the larger issues of confidentiality and referral. SEXUALITY ISSUES Working with Gender Boundaries The forth critical boundary issues in ministry-related counseling con- cerns gender and sexuality. We live in a society obsessed with sexuality, no less in the church than in the secular world. The Christian church has 10 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING certainly seen its share of moral failures and adulterous relationships. Such failures damage, not only the local congregation, but the reputa- tion and credibility of the larger faith community. Congregations and leadership have rightly become highly concerned with issues of sexual- ity and reputation. Given that leadership in many Christian ministries is predominantly male, the issue of male-female relationships becomes paramount. Anecdotal evidence would indicate that the majority of con- gregants in Christian churches are female, which creates a difficult boundary issue for all aspects of ministry. Counseling ministries, in particular, become vulnerable because of the intimate nature of the content and process. The prevalence and publicity of sexual misconduct among clergy and ministry counselors has led to increasing rigidity in ministry and counsel- ing roles. After reviewing a number of studies, Thoburn and Balswick (1998) found that clergy have the highest rate of sexual contact among pro- fessional people helpers. While the statistics make it clear that a pastor is more likely to have extra-marital sexual contact with a church member or friend than with a member of the church staff or with a counselee, the norm for extra-marital relationships with counselees involves long-term emo- tional investment, rather than impulsive moral lapse (Thoburn & Balswick, 1998). Such findings make it critical to assess initial boundary crossings carefully and set up appropriate accountability structures proactively, rather than reactively. However such accountability must take into account both ministerial protection and the reality of shepherding a gender diverse community. An over-reliance on detailed rules can become restrictive of genuine relationship between genders in our churches. While well intentioned and even necessary at times, such over-reliance can potentially hinder true Christian intimacy, as well as genuine healing ministry. Rather than following Jesus’ example of a life of integrity and personal accountabil- ity, we often choose the easier way of the Pharisees, multiplying rules and restrictions which can limit rather than build healthy relationships. Simply abstaining from various actions in any and all circumstances may provide a limited prescription for safe practice, but it does not nec- essarily lead to either godly ministry or effective counseling. Our ac- tions should flow from the sincerity of a Christlike character, tempered with wisdom that comes from above (Ja 1:5; 3:17). Knowing when to say “no,” when to seek godly counsel, and when to extend a boundary in a limited circumstance takes much discernment. A brief pastoral visit to a recently bereaved spouse of the opposite gender may be an appropri- Miriam Stark Parent 11 ate boundary extension, although normative practice may not include home visits without accompaniment to opposite gender congregants. In legitimately attempting to safeguard against clergy misconduct, some clergy have chosen to exclude all counseling or visitation. Some have policies which preclude ever closing a door for private conversation with a congregant of the opposite sex. While well-intentioned and some- times even necessary, such policies may severely limit the shepherding aspects of ministry to public, non-relational venues. Some have sought accountability by never ministering alone, particularly in counseling ses- sions. While mega-churches and ministries may have the resources nec- essary, this is often unrealistic for the average parish ministry. In addition, confidentiality and legal privilege become moot as there can be no legal confidentiality (i.e., privilege) when a third party is present. Hav- ing a spouse, secretary or other woman sit in on counseling done by male leadership, can also preclude any sense of safety for the female congre- gant. Unfortunately, the subtle message conveyed is often one of moral danger and sexual awareness, rather than acceptance and spiritual con- cern. The argument that it is for the counselee’s protection implies either an unsafe counselor or a hierarchal power dynamic inappropriate in a counseling ministry. Standard policies that subtly convey inappropriate messages about either the counselor’s vulnerability or the client’s sexual- ity need to be carefully assessed. The absence of safe Christian intimacy can destroy a counseling ministry far faster than a false allegation made in the face of an untarnished reputation. While the scope of public ministry, personal vulnerability or specific cultural views about male-female interactions may dictate such poli- cies, the assumptions behind them need to be carefully thought through and articulated. Some churches have arranged to have pastoral counsel- ing staff of both genders available for spiritual and personal guidance. Whatever approach the church or ministry chooses to take, the ramifica- tions must be carefully assessed and the policies clearly articulated to the congregation to avoid the type of misunderstandings and differing expectations that can so easily destroy true community and ministry. In many counseling ministry settings, wisdom may readily dictate that doors with narrow window panels be installed or offices with win- dows be used for counseling. While confidentiality and privacy can still be maintained with translucent window coverings, the acceptance of ac- countability to the greater church community is made explicit. Policies regarding the presence of others in the immediate vicinity or in the facil- ity may also be considered as appropriate accountability structures. Normative boundaries concerning time and place of counseling ap- 12 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING pointments need to be made explicit, particularly in small church set- tings. Issues of home visitations need careful documentation and plan- ning for the safety of all concerned. But such things ought not to be sum- marily discarded if we are genuinely to care and minister in faith communities. Working with Youth and Children These days gender is not the only place where issues of sexuality are raised in church counseling venues. The sexual abuse of children by those in positions of spiritual authority has also raised critical concerns for ministry-related counseling. Sheler (1992) has noted that the reports of clergy sexual abuse are on the increase across the religious landscape, from Protestant and Mormon churches to Jewish, Muslim and Buddhist congregations and the emerging numbers are staggering. Those who would abuse have all too often found our children easily accessible and adults to ready to disbelieve. Churches should certainly be the safest places for children. We must not allow a naive emphasis on God’s trans- forming grace and redemption to be separated from firm convictions about the deceitfulness of sin. If we do, we may fail to comprehend the multiplying dangers of child abusers, even in our churches. In response some churches have found themselves in the dilemma of preaching the importance of a father’s involvement in parenting and then excluding all males from serving in the nursery, even in the com- pany of their wives, or working with young children in any capacity. Seeking wisdom in the creation of policies that protect our children is no less difficult than in dealing with gender issues. Well crafted policies that fit an individual ministry’s needs can set healthy boundaries that define and nurture generational relationships. Hasty or arbitrary poli- cies designed out of fear or dictated by liability concerns emerge as rigid rules, carrying subtle messages about moral fitness and lack of safety. Screening potential staff and volunteers has become necessary and commonplace in ministry settings. To naively accept on faith another’s assertion of innocence may not be acceptable these days, especially as it relates to working with children. Routine criminal background checks are encouraged, if not mandated, even for volunteer staff. Policies with clear and adequate rationale are generally accepted without congrega- tional complaint. Ministry counselors are often entrusted with obtaining this information or crafting solutions to difficult ministry situations that arise out of such information or policies. In such situations, a ministry counselor may find himself or herself holding more and more problem- Miriam Stark Parent 13 atic information and seeking realistic solutions that will truly heal rather than further damage someone seeking help. Boundaries that are flexible allow ministers and counselors to deter- mine when it is necessary to cross a boundary and to maximize the use of existing accountability structures in doing so. Stretching a boundary after thorough reflection may have a beneficial effect far beyond the im- mediate situation. The youth counselor who determines there is a need for one-on-one time with a particular teen outside the church office in a less formal setting, may open the door to some life-threatening and, thereby, life-changing disclosures. With well-designed accountability measures in place (e.g., immediate supervisor notification) such unus- ual boundary crossings need not incur significant risk. CONFIDENTIALITY ISSUES Throughout the Scriptures the sins of the tongue are given prominence, perhaps because they are so deadly. Proverbs 20:19 reminds us that “A gossip betrays a confidence, so avoid a man who talks too much.” Pastors and counselors are often afforded the great gift of free access to the “hid- den heart” of individuals they counsel. With that responsibility comes the expectation that what they learn, they will use graciously and carefully. Rarely do those in counseling ministries ever intend to do otherwise, yet violating confidentiality is the most common boundary violation of clergy or counselor. Fortunately, it is not often harmful and generally is overlooked or unknown. It results from careless conversation, providing too much identifying information in an illustration, confiding details to a spouse or accountability partner without the other person’s consent, or a hundred other ways that the tongue runs ahead of careful thought. Respecting Information The expectation of trust is so great in helping relationships that both clergy and counselors are granted protection by law that limits the infor- mation they can be forced to divulge, even by the government. While there have been increasing limitations placed on that protection, it is still generally recognized. In the United States, communications between a clergy and parishioner or a licensed mental health counselor and a counselee are considered privileged communications and protected by law. In the past this privilege has been more widely understood. How- ever, with increasing litigation has come a more narrow definition which 14 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING generally uses ordination or state licensure by a professional board as a determinant of privileged communication. Conversations with peer or lay counselors, church staff or parachurch workers, while expected to be con- fidential, are not generally accorded the legal protection of privileged communication. This legal protection mandates that unless limitations are agreed upon in advance or written into law, only the parishioner/counselee may determine who is given access to that information, including family members. This has direct implications for those doing counseling in ministries where issues of church discipline or corporate community standards are enacted. It may be too late to seek permission to pass on information (e.g., an ongoing affair) after it has been disclosed. Bound- aries around the sharing of information need to be agreed upon prior to any disclosures in order to be effective. Youth counselors are frequently attempting to balance fragile teenage trust and parental concern. Minis- try policies about what information might be shared need to be made explicit and agreed upon by both teens and parents. The sharing of intimate information is inherent in counseling, but ap- propriate boundaries may differ from counselor to counselee. What may seem inconsequential to the counselor may be deeply held by the counselee. A seemingly innocuous illustration used publicly can easily become grounds for breach of trust allegations within a ministry. Once trust is legitimately challenged, it may take a long time to rebuild an ef- fective ministry. Consequently, respecting information shared within a counseling ministry context is crucial. Written Documentation Technology has brought us into the information age. It has also changed how we handle information. In previous years personal mem- ory was a sufficient standard–if a respected authority (e.g., doctor, clergy, counselor) said it was so, it was. That is no longer true. In an age of individual equality and skepticism of public leadership, anyone’s word needs to be backed up with documentation. Formal counseling re- lationships require keeping concise but thorough records. Written con- sent to policies or notes indicating that a verbal agreement was reached become essential documentation when crises emerge. Time and activity logs, along with concise notes on session content, need to be maintained in a confidential format. In ministries where offices are often highly ac- cessible, counseling files need special protection. The counselor is ulti- mately responsible for the actions of anyone who might access those Miriam Stark Parent 15 files. Although staff confidentiality and integrity should be legitimate expectations, wisdom dictates limiting temptation by carefully securing any counseling files. While lawyers advocate keeping records as good risk management, the principle goes much deeper. Keeping records makes counselors more aware and, consequently, better at what they do. When we review and document our activities, we become aware of dangerous patterns, overlooked information and other ways in which we might improve our ministry. Informal and routine counseling relationships also need to be docu- mented. Ministers who regularly do premarital counseling often neglect to keep sufficient record of the nature and content of individual ses- sions. Crisis counseling often starts and ends with a lengthy phone call, but may include life threatening or life changing information. While formal files may not be necessary, keeping a personal log of such inter- ventions should be routine for anyone in ministry. Good accountability structures include keeping close track of both phone and visitation rec- ords, as well as appointment calendars. Clear boundaries, combined with objective and wise documentation, can stop a firestorm that might burn out of control when fueled by ambivalence, lack of memory, and subjective evaluations. Competing Information Demands For many years professional counselors have been mandated by laws enacted in each state and province in North America to report any sus- pected neglect or abuse of a minor by a person responsible for the care of that child when that information comes to them in their professional capacity. Recognizing that individuals do not have the capability or fa- cilities to investigate such claims, states encouraged all persons to re- port any suspicion of abuse and protected the individual from charges of slander if the charges were not substantiated, but made in good faith. People in professions who routinely interact with children (e.g., teach- ers, counselors, doctors) are not only encouraged but required to report any suspicion. In these cases, counselor/client privilege was non-exis- tent. In recent years this reporting has been expanded to include report- ing suspected abuse of dependent or older adults who are not able to protect themselves from their caretakers. Until recently clergy have been exempt from such requirements. Based on the model of the Roman Catholic confessional, clergy com- munications have always carried the highest legal safeguards. This be- 16 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING gan to erode very quickly in the early 1990s as child abusers found churches to be vulnerable in their faith in redemption and their unwill- ingness to believe a child’s report without adult validation. Among oth- ers, adult survivors who reported that they told ministry adults about abuse when they were children only to be disbelieved or have these sins covered up, have successfully advocated for change. State laws are be- ing rewritten quickly to include clergy as mandated reporters of child abuse. At this writing, 18 states require all persons to report and 25 states specifically mandate clergy as reporters (see http://nccanch.acf. hhs.gov for updated information). With only three states overlapping, that means 40 states currently require clergy to report suspected child abuse or neglect by a caregiver. This has led to real concern about the role of clergy and ministerial counselors in confession and repentance. While most states explicitly cite a clergy/penitent exception to reporting, five states have recently denied that privilege. When it is granted, two criteria are required to meet the exemption. The clergy must be in a pastoral role (i.e., ordained or recognized spiritual leader) and the information must have come through a minister-penitent relationship. If a child comes to a minister and tells of abuse happening, this is not a penitent relationship. How- ever, “ ...ifaman goes to his pastor and confesses that he has sexually abused his child, that he is repentant and wants to “get right with God,” the abuse does not have to be reported. Two conditions exist that protect the confidentiality of the communication: first, the minister has been ap- proached in a pastoral role, and second, the confession is penitential in nature” (Levicoff, 1991,122). The counseling role must be differenti- ated from the confessional role. Disclosure in the process of marital counseling may not be protected. Likewise, disclosure to a lay coun- selor or elder is not protected as the person is not considered clergy. Po- tential counselees need to understand the boundaries and limitations of confidentiality before counseling begins, not after a disclosure has been made. When there is an allegation of abuse, a report is made to the appropri- ate state agency, not just to a parent. Whether or not to immediately no- tify the parents may depend on whether they are involved (as opposed to someone else in a caregiving capacity, such as a teacher), the nature of the abuse, the family relationship, and ministry policies among many other variables. While ministries struggle with a real understanding of repentance and redemption, there is also justifiable concern about recid- ivism rates for child abuse, which are among the highest for any crime. We rejoice in the Holy Spirit’s transforming work, but we must also rec- Miriam Stark Parent 17 ognize that accepting societal consequences may be a part of that trans- forming process. Knowing and understanding the pertinent state law is essential. Each state and province has a slightly different wording and may vary the pro- cess in some manner. Most allow for an anonymous phone consult with the state agency when circumstances are uncertain. However, if the cir- cumstances are judged to be reportable, a written report is generally ex- pected within 72 hours. Illinois has a manual available online for those individuals designated as mandated reporters. It is written clearly and lays out both process and responsibilities clearly (see www.state.il. us/dcfs/docs/MANDATED2002.pdf). Other states increasingly have simi- lar documents available online. Clergy and church counselors no longer have the option of ignorance in these matters. Some ministries have sought out mental health profes- sionals to provide general information to ministerial staff, offer crisis supervision or provide informational meetings for congregants. For ministry counselors, forging a relationship with the appropriate local agency can be a proactive way of engaging the community, as well as balancing civil requirements with good shepherding. COMPETENCY ISSUES At the beginning of the 20th century, competency was usually a matter of character and actions. In small communities a person was sought out because he or she had lived life well or had excelled in some specific area. That individual was considered competent to handle the task being pre- sented. At the beginning of the 21st century, competence is more likely to be based on education and credentials. With a mobile, often anonymous society, longitudinal subjective assessment has given way to more imme- diate objective criteria. In ministry and in counseling, intuitive people skills crafted by graduate training in theory and practice and, hopefully, enabled by the nurture of the Holy Spirit, form a solid basis for effective ministry. One without the others can present challenges that must be ad- dressed. Credentials in counseling often differ from those required by the pro- fessional ministry degree, Master of Divinity. At some denominational seminaries the M.Div. requires a full year of people and counseling re- lated courses (30+ semester hours). However, in many seminaries there is little specific counseling coursework (3+ semester hours) required. This has left many churches in a difficult position of expecting un- 18 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING trained, sometimes incompetent, ministers to offer appropriate counsel- ing for any of a variety of problematic individual, marital and family issues. Many times intuitive people skills and solid life experience, nur- tured by the Holy Spirit, have brought healing and help to those in need. In other situations, clergy have turned to others in the church and com- munity to provide the counseling ministry. At other times some have simply muddled through leaving hurt people more damaged by their lack of understanding. As with any profession (e.g., medical, legal, accounting) professional counselors are licensed by the state in which they practice. This ascer- tains that they have met certain basic requirements; it does not necessar- ily mean they are competent. It implies that they have either a master’s degree or a doctoral degree in counseling, have passed certain knowl- edge and practice-based exams and have practiced under supervision for at least two years. Most states do not permit persons who do not hold a counseling license to practice professional or clinical counseling, de- pending on how the state defines it. Those in counseling ministries who are not licensed may offer peer, lay, pastoral, spiritual or other types of counseling; but they may not hold themselves out as mental health professionals who do clinical or professional counseling. The law requires only that the counselor imply credentials and train- ing accurately. While some willfully intend to defraud insurance com- panies or individuals, others may sincerely believe that they are qualified by matter of position rather than training. If so, this must be spelled out carefully in order to be clear about the kind of services being offered. This is the counselor’s responsibility and is in accord with the emphasis on integrity placed on ministers of God’s word in Scripture. Philippians 2:15 calls us to “ ...be blameless and innocent, children of God above reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you appear as lights in the world.” Recognition of Competence Persons involved in any type of counseling ministry must recognize both their gifts and their limitations. Neither pride nor false humility serve the community of God. Where God calls us to intervene, he will provide the necessary resources. Often our mistake is in assuming that we are that resource, rather than recognizing our own boundaries and understanding our service of referral. Each person involved in counseling ministry needs to assess their own areas of competency and its boundaries. Some are highly competent in Miriam Stark Parent 19 theareaof Biblical or theological understanding. They know the Scrip- tures well and are able to provide good teaching and understanding on difficult topics such as divorce, homosexuality, and marriage roles among others. Many fine Christians who engage in counseling ministry are well equipped in other areas, but lack a clear understanding or knowl- edge of Scripture or relevant theological doctrines. A referral to the teach- ing pastor for counsel on a particular issue may be an essential part of the healing process. Going with the individual for that session may be hum- bling, but could result in both being blessed by the information and the in- teraction with that learning. Cultural competence is another area that must be assessed. As our churches and ministries have become increasingly diverse, counselors must ask themselves if they truly understand the ethnic or racial impli- cations of their counsel. To understand what it means to be Afri- can-American in a white, suburban church may be a necessary pre- cursor to bringing healing to a specific situation or family. If culture is extended to include issues of diversity, competence may be further challenged by biases about the role of the elderly, teen culture, gender, socioeconomic class, or a variety of other issues. Maturity may demand admitting a lack of understanding and seeking out someone with more expertise or one who can offer supervision for this situation. Lay or peer counseling ministries can be a vital asset in the church and in faith communities. Members of the body of Christ are called to support one another. However, given the professionalization of helping services and the increase of church litigation, this is an area that calls for wise planning in setting appropriate boundaries. Competence in coun- seling ministry means more than just being a nice person. Counselors must be equipped with certain skills. They need to be able to recognize when problems reach beyond workable solutions or involve more pro- found changes than can be made with the support available. Active lis- tening is a learned skill that must be practiced, even in lay counseling. Church staff and volunteers alike must be willing to understand and articulate the kinds of situations they are prepared to work with and those they are not. The level and amount of training must be appropriate to service. Lay counselors need to be screened, trained and supervised by someone with greater training, as well as discernment. When the boundary of a counselor’s competence has been reached, there must be an appropriate referral to someone qualified to deal with that situation. Personal competence is also a necessary assessment for any counsel- ing minister. Some people desire to help others only for the ego satisfac- tion it brings them. Others genuinely desire to help, but are ill equipped 20 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING to handle the stresses of life themselves, let alone provide stability for others. The question of spiritual giftedness and emotional fit must be weighed against a need to rescue and fix everyone–sometimes referred to as a Messiah complex. Good counselors do not necessarily “have it all together,” but they are aware of their weaknesses and willing to work on them. Sometimes God uses someone who has struggled in a similar area to truly understand the weaknesses of another of His children. However, in some situations that same understanding may become a li- ability if it draws the counselor back into his or her own struggle. Where there is great similarity or great discrepancy in life experiences, coun- seling is often difficult. Too much similarity may make it difficult for the counselee to be heard uniquely and clearly. Too much discrepancy may limit the necessary understanding each must offer the other. Resource and Referral Recognizing the boundaries of competence does not mean walking away or abandoning someone in need. Implying that their situation is too difficult may do more harm. An appropriate referral means offering a better option to deal with a particular situation. Finding the right re- source means knowing the options available in both the larger faith community and the secular community. When an appropriate referral is not immediately clear, there needs to be a person or facility available with the competence to evaluate and make the necessary referral. Resources may include community mental health centers which often provide low-cost, ongoing counseling for difficult family situations and chronic mental illness. They also run, as do hospitals, various kinds of support and psychoeducational groups on either a time-limited or ongo- ing basis. Doctors who can evaluate the need for and prescribe medica- tions may be either psychiatrists or skilled family practitioners. Com- munity social agencies may be sources of specific assistance for housing or crisis needs that are beyond the scope of the church or ministry. Trauma services with 24 hour involvement and support staff (e.g., Rape Companion programs) may extend ministry services. Ministries are often reluctant to refer to outside counseling resources as they fear losing all contact or control over the individuals. While this may happen, it is more often caused by lack of foresight and knowledge than intent. Because of confidentiality requirements, contact is often cut off and ministry counselors feel left out after a referral. If the counselee is willing, a simple release of information form can be signed and a copy provided to the new counselor. The counselee’s signature indi- Miriam Stark Parent 21 cates that he or she is granting permission for the ministry counselor to provide information (which may be specified as to content) to the new counselor or agency. If they sign a similar agreement with the commu- nity counselor or doctor, that individual will be able in return to provide specified information back to the ministry counselor or pastor. While it is entirely at the counselee’s discretion, it must be done in writing for each party involved in order for two-way communication to take place. The type of information given and received is usually limited to whether or not the counselee followed through with the placement and generally how the process is going, including any way the church or ministry may assist. Having an existing relationship with individuals at various commu- nity agencies, as well as other referral sources, can ease the transition of counseling and facilitate the communication process to the benefit of all involved. Open discussion about the possible benefits of referral and knowledgeable input about the resource will help the counselee to feel assisted rather than that he or she is too much to handle and is being abandoned. Following up with the counselee or possibly assisting them in making the connection to the new resource can be a great assistance and calm any initial fears or misapprehensions. CONCLUSION There is an oft quoted line from Robert Frost that “Good fences make good neighbors” (Lathem, 1979). The principle of establishing clear boundaries to facilitate good relationships is a wise one, if not always an easy one. Being explicit about our roles and responsibilities facilitates good stewardship of our time and ministry in counseling. Being proac- tive in our counseling ministries allows us the freedom to concentrate on the individual’s immediate crisis or growth rather than having to take time to focus on our own situation. Where policies and structures exist, they can easily be adapted to meet the current demand; when they must be created on the spot, we run high risk of setting poor policies or de- faulting to sometimes rigid rules that protect, but may not heal. The key to boundary issues is thoughtfulness and critical awareness. When practice diverges from policy, it is important to know why it is nec- essary and to be able to enact appropriate accountability structures. A rapid return to customary practice is critical. Ministries to individuals cannot solely be dictated by rules; there are too many variables. Wisdom is a fluid process, requiring assessment and evaluation of each situation in light of 22 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING well-designed policies. Critical awareness of warning signals is essential in monitoring our counseling and keeping our ministry boundaries appropri- ate to the setting and service where God has placed us. Calculate the Cost Biblical stewardship of our reputation, as well as our time and talents, requires that we consider carefully any boundary extensions that we feel necessary to make in our counseling relationships. When normative boundaries have been consistently and clearly established, then it is easy to discern when a boundary has been reached. Wisdom dictates that we should not proceed impulsively, but carefully calculate the cost involved. Jesus’ discussion of the cost of discipleship in Luke 14:28-30 is one such reminder in Scripture. If the object is to serve, rather than to be served, to do no harm, and to bring healing when possible, it is criti- cal to assess any departure from normative practice carefully. The following four simple questions might serve to facilitate our work and preclude much of the negative outcome that often results from impulsive boundary crossing. 1. Is the outcome worth the risk? This is the basic assessment ques- tion that must be answered. Simply being asked to do something that takes us beyond our regular boundaries, such as meeting at unusual times, does not necessarily mandate an affirmative re- sponse. Sometimes the risk of a boundary extension being misun- derstood by the counselee and thereby doing harm, means that the request cannot be granted. Sometimes the ministry risk in a partic- ular situation is simply too high. 2. Am I being led by the Holy Spirit or personal needs? Even asking the question dictates an awareness of personal areas of vulnerabil- ity. Counseling relationships can create powerful temptation for inappropriately meeting the counselor’s needs. Unless carefully guarded against, we may be too deaf to hear the clear voice of the Holy Spirit or too blind to see where we are headed. Sometimes it is necessary to seek outside wisdom or consultation as we can eas- ily be misled by our own desires. 3. Is there a less risky alternative? Because one answer immediately appears to be best does not mean it necessarily is the best or that it is the only answer. Other options may be available and advisable. A thoughtful response, rather than an immediate one, may be the better answer. Allowing some time, even if only a few moments, Miriam Stark Parent 23 before answering can be critical. Consultation may present an easy solution that we did not have the clarity or the knowledge to see. 4. If the boundary crossing seems necessary, then the question must be asked: How can I minimize the risk? Much is said in the church these days concerning accountability structures, but action must follow discussion. For the church-related counseling ministry, as indeed for all of us, there needs to be clear accountability struc- tures which are regularly used. A simple phone call to alert a su- pervisor or colleague of an intentional boundary crossing and the reasons for it may avert a host of misunderstandings.
