What is our response to leaders within the community of faith who have become involved in some behavior that results in dam- age to themselves and others in the community? In this article, we examine factors that may be associated with restor- ing leaders to wholeness. Clearly, leaders in society may harm them- selves (e.g., by drugs) and others (e.g., by violence, deceit) in many ways. We have restricted our focus to pastors who have had extramari- tal affairs within a community of faith. We selected this problem as a proxy for the troublesome impact that a leader’s behavior can cause for the leader, spouse, children, friends, and community (i.e., congregants). Thoburn and Balswick (1998) analyzed data from 186 male seminari- ans representing 23 denominations. They found that 15.6% engaged in extramarital sexual activity. Most sexual activity was between a pastor and a church member, but sexual intercourse was primarily between a pastor and a counselee. More recently, researchers from the Hartford In- stitute for Religion Research (2000) found that 23% of 532 Christian congregations experienced a pastor-congregation disruption due to a pastor’s sexual activity. We begin the exploration of our topic by examining a model for wholeness and then examining the concepts of transgression and re- sponse, forgiveness, reconciliation, and restoration. We conclude by noting implications for practice and research. SCOPES: A MODEL FOR WHOLENESS To set the stage for our later discussion, we first turn to a model of wholeness that adds a spiritual dimension to many of the elements typi- cally considered by cognitive-behavioral psychotherapists (e.g., Beck, 1979; Beck & Beck, 1995). We use the acronym SCOPES to represent a wholistic model that focuses on the unity of a person but with multidi- mensional aspects of functioning. The model is somewhat similar to Lazarus’ model described in his writings on multimodal therapy (e.g., Lazarus, 1989). First, in the spiritual (S) dimension, a person recognizes 28 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING a deeply felt lack of wholeness and a need for deep communion with an- other being. Second, cognition (C) involves thinking as represented by both verbal and nonverbal (or imaginal) cognitions. Verbal cognitions include beliefs and opinions, as well as transient thoughts. Third, overt (O) behavior largely reflects that aspect of functioning seen by others and often examined as an index of intrapersonal functioning. Fourth, the physical (P) domain represents the biological basis of behavior. Physi- cal functioning may include general health variables such as heart rate, strength, and muscle tone; disease entities such as cancer and diabetes; and more specific variables associated with psychological functioning such as genetic findings, hormone levels, and neurotransmitter levels. Fifth, emotional (E) functioning represents that rather hidden domain that we refer to by positive terms such as happiness and satisfaction, as well as negative emotional states such as anger and fear. Finally, we rec- ognize that people do not exist alone, but in some social (S) network that varies considerably but often includes a romantic partner, children, close relatives, friends, and associates in a community such as cowork- ers and committee members. In the context of this paper, restoration to wholeness means a return to a state of wholeness that existed before a transgression event that appears to be the proximal cause for a disrup- tion in one or more domains of functioning. Although a useful goal, it is probably unrealistic to think that we could help people attain some heightened level of wholeness that did not exist in the leader’s recent history. However, it may be reasonable to consider that, once on a path to restoration, a leader could continue to grow and develop after a formal community-initiated restoration process concluded. TRANSGRESSION AND RESPONSE Conceptualizations of Transgression and Response When considering the restoration process within a community of faith, we are forced to ask the obvious question, “What happened?” What event or series of events has occurred that prompts consideration of restoration? In the forgiveness literature, an offensive event has been referred to as a transgression (e.g., Fincham, Jackson, & Beach, in press; Thompson, Snyder, Hoffman, Michael, Rasmussen, Billings et al., in press). We con- tinue the use of the term transgression and note that such a stimulus event, if it were the cause for some degree of restoration, would also be called a stressor. As noted above, although a leader can offend a community in Geoffrey W. Sutton and Eloise K. Thomas 29 many ways, we decided to focus on an extramarital affair. The transgres- sion clearly has an impact on the leader, but the offender has not been studied as much as the victim has. In addition to the type of offense, we may also examine other dimensions such as frequency and duration, as well as offender characteristics and posttransgression responses. Trans- gression events have also been examined for subjective and objective ef- fects (Fincham et al., in press). More likely than not, a transgression, such as an extramarital affair, will result in various stress responses among the members of the faith community. Typically, concern has focused on the victims of offense, but when we consider the possibility of restoring a leader to wholeness, the impact on both the leader and the victims must be considered. Sev- eral forgiveness researchers have studied the impact of a transgression on victims using the term unforgiveness explained by Worthington and his colleagues as a set of emotions such as resentment, bitterness, ha- tred, hostility, anger, and fear (see e.g., Worthington & Wade, 1999; Worthington, Berry, & Parrott, 2001). The condition of unforgiveness develops only within those who ruminate (Worthington & Scherer, 2004). Once it is developed, victims perceive unforgiveness as stressful and may experience physiological effects similar to other stressors. Vic- tims may reduce this unforgiveness-stress condition in many ways other than forgiveness (Worthington & Scherer, 2004). Commentary on Transgression and Response The term transgression adds a moral connotation to a stressor and implies a need to balance the books of justice for this unfair intrusion into one’s life. The term is somewhat advantageous for Christians who are used to asking forgiveness for their own transgressions against a just God and, thus, may enhance understanding of the relationship problem caused by the leader’s transgression within the community. In contrast, the general public does not use the term unforgiveness. This leaves cli- nicians and researchers with the task of explaining the nuances of unforgiveness and describing the possible boundary conditions that dis- tinguish it from other stress responses. Given the various ways that unforgiveness can be addressed, a term analogous to PTSD such as Transgression Response Stress Syndrome (TRSS) may be more under- standable to those unfamiliar with the forgiveness literature, including clients and research participants. A term such as TRSS uses understand- able concepts of stress and transgression and allows for researchers, clinicians, and theorists to identify the features likely characteristic of 30 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING the syndrome (i.e., unforgiveness). Conceptually, researchers present unforgiveness as a motivational state. Although effort has been directed at understanding the process of forgiveness, little has been written about a process of unforgiveness. Rather, unforgiveness appears to be the result of the rumination process, which is also a concept in need of fur- ther exploration. FORGIVENESS, FORGIVING, AND FORGIVER Conceptualizations of Forgiveness, Forgiving, and Forgiver It has become axiomatic among forgiveness researchers that there is no agreement on a conceptual definition (e.g., Fincham & Kashdan, in press; Thompson et al., in press; Worthington & Scherer, 2004) but that there is an emerging core of forgiveness attributes (Worthington & Scherer, 2004) that appear to involve a transformation of motivations following a transgression (e.g., Fincham & Kashdan, in press; McCullough, Fincham, & Tsang, 2003). We considered formulations by researchers who have examined various as- pects of forgiveness in empirical studies. Enright and Gassin (1992) consid- ered forgiveness to be a complex phenomenon that included affective, cognitive, and behavioral systems. In the process of forgiveness, a person works to replace negative responses (affects, cognitions, and behaviors) with positive responses. McCullough, Rachal, Sandage, Worthington, Brown, and Hight (1998) posited that forgiving involves a transformation in which a victim reduces avoidance and revenge motivations following a transgres- sion. Their index of forgiveness, Transgression-Related Interpersonal Moti- vations (TRIM), includes two subscales of avoidance and revenge, con- sistent with their theorizing. Elsewhere, McCullough and his colleagues (2003) noted a positive element in which a person develops conciliatory mo- tivations toward the offender. Worthington and Scherer (2004) have pro- posed two types of forgiveness, emotional forgiveness and decisional forgiveness, and note that their work has focused on emotional forgiveness. Thompson et al. (2004) defined forgiveness as a dialectical process in which a person reframes a perceived transgression in a way that shifts the responses from negative to neutral or positive. Gordon, Baucom et al. (2004) have in- corporated their three-component model of forgiveness into a relationship treatment program. Forgiveness progresses from a realistic appraisal of the relationship, to a release from control by negative affect, and ultimately to a reduced motivation to punish the offender. Geoffrey W. Sutton and Eloise K. Thomas 31 A useful approach to understanding the current conceptualizations of forgiveness is to consider what forgiveness is not (Fincham, Beach, & Davila, 2004; Fincham & Kashdan, in press). It seems most would agree that forgiveness is not denying, condoning, pardoning, forgetting, or reconciling. Researchers have begun to examine forgiveness as a personality trait that is dispositional forgiveness. Berry, Worthington, Parrott, O’Connor, and Wade (2001) found dispositional forgiveness, measured by the Transgression Narrative Test of Forgiveness (TNFT), to be negatively correlated with anger and neuroticism and positively correlated with agreeableness in several student samples. Brown and Phillips (2004) found that the Tendency to Forgive (TTF) scale predicted mental health variables of depression and life-satisfaction, as well as state forgiveness, for a recalled offense in an undergraduate sample. Commentary on Forgiveness, Forgiving, and Forgiver The lack of a consensus definition for forgiveness is not surprising given the early stages of research. It seems reasonable to view forgive- ness as a multidimensional, motivational construct. One area of differ- ence for some researchers is whether the state of neutrality constitutes forgiveness. That is, most agree that forgiveness entails letting go of negative emotions and cognitions, but researchers do not agree whether forgiveness requires the presence of positive emotions and cognitions. The differences are not trivial because they have driven both research (McCullough et al., 1998) and treatment (e.g., Gordon, Baucom et al.). A recent study by Fincham and colleagues (2004) suggested support for a three-part conceptualization of forgiveness (retaliation, avoidance, and benevolence) that operated differently for married men than for married women. Laypeople do not distinguish between forgiveness as an intraper- sonal process and reconciliation as an interpersonal process (Kantz, 2000). Researchers appear to have made a consistent effort at separating these two concepts in the forgiveness literature. Nevertheless, when concepts are conflated in the general population, clinicians and re- searchers will be in a position of constantly explaining how their propri- etary definitions differ from those of their clients or participants. The purpose of the distinction seems reasonable. It would be dangerous for clients to return to abusive partners because they believed that forgive- ness required reconciliation. Although forgiveness has an interpersonal context, it is clearly an intrapersonal event in the view of most research- 32 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING ers. The importance of the conceptual difference suggests it should be on the list for public education efforts as suggested by Fincham and Kashdan (in press). The early studies of dispositional forgiveness suggest a promising di- rection for additional research. The correlation with Big Five Traits offers the potential for clinicians to consider the personality characteristics of those seeking treatment for concerns that include interpersonal transgres- sions. Presumably, those with a tendency to forgive may be more respon- sive to forgiveness interventions. One aspect that has not been addressed is the general latency of response. Researchers have studied the tendency to forgive but have not studied how quickly the participants forgave an offense. We would expect people high in dispositional forgiveness to have both a higher rate of forgiveness and a shorter latency of response than those low in dispositional forgiveness. Another dimension of forgiveness that has not been directly addressed by the existing literature is that of state versus process conceptualizations of forgiveness. Presumably, most would agree that forgiveness can be achieved. When it is achieved, people are in a state of forgiveness. They have reached a point that they no longer struggle with the negative effects of the transgression; instead, they experience positive emotions when considering the offender and the offense. However, most of the research focusing on the process of forgiving has used scales that measure a range of values that suggest where a person falls on a continuum from no for- giveness to complete forgiveness. In addition, research has focused on correlates of the forgiving process and variables that may promote forgiv- ing. We propose that the subtle difference between a state of forgiveness and a process of forgiving is a meaningful difference that needs to be ad- dressed in treatment and research. In addition to conceptualizing the vari- ous aspects of forgiveness as has been done, we suggest clinicians and researchers alike should focus on the similarities or differences between those who are at various stages in the process of forgiving and those who have completed a forgiveness process. This may become viable when re- search moves beyond the focus on forgiving in a dyadic context to forgiv- ing in a small group or community context. We propose different definitions of forgiveness (state) and forgiving (process) that account for state and process conceptualizations respec- tively. Forgiveness is a multidimensional intrapersonal relational con- cept. It is a reasonably stable, motivational state that exists when a person experiences positive cognitive, affective, and/or physiological responses toward offenders and/or their transgressions. The state of for- Geoffrey W. Sutton and Eloise K. Thomas 33 giveness follows a choice to forgive that occurs sometime during the forgiving process. Forgiving is a multidimensional, motivational pro- cess that reflects overall increasing positive changes in cognitive, affective, and/or physiological responses toward offenders and/or their trans- gressions. The process has a starting point following a transgression. The process may be interrupted or reversed. The process may or may not result in a stable state of forgiveness. In addition, we propose a definition of dispositional forgiveness that reflects a pattern of forgiving in terms of frequency and latency of forgiving responses. Dispositional forgiveness is a personality trait that reflects a tendency to respond to many transgressions with posi- tive cognitions, affects, and/or physiological states within a short time frame. RECONCILING AND RECONCILIATION Conceptualizations of Reconciling and Reconciliation Any understanding of restoring a person to wholeness following a stressful event must consider the interpersonal relationships that have been damaged or lost. The forgiveness literature has largely focused on intrapersonal responses to interpersonal transgression events. In contrast, reconciliation focuses on the restoration of relationships. Several writers have drawn a clear distinction between the concepts of forgiveness and reconciliation (Enright & Cole, 1998; Worthington, 1998; Worthington, 2000; Worthington & Drinkard, 2000; Worthington & Wade, 1999). Enright and Coyle (1998) separated the concepts of forgiveness and rec- onciliation when they noted that a person could forgive an offender yet elect not to be in a relationship with that person. When they suggested that forgiveness might lead to reconciliation between an injured party and an offender, they seemed to view forgiveness as a precursor to reconcilia- tion. They clearly saw the concepts of forgiveness and reconciliation as exclusive but related ideas. Worthington and Drinkard (2000) found little empirical research on reconciliation in human relationships. Drawing on diverse literatures, they suggested a theoretical six-step model for pro- moting reconciliation in couples. They contrasted the concept of forgive- ness (an intrapersonal process) with that of reconciliation (an inter- personal process). In addition, they suggested that much reconciliation occurs with limited awareness of the steps taken to reconcile and thus may be considered implicit reconciliation in contrast with their proposed 34 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING intervention approach, explicit reconciliation. Sandage, Worthington, Hight, and Berry (2000) related forgiveness to the reconciliation process when they discussed the concept of seeking forgiveness as a motivational construct that included cognition (e.g., the perspective of the victim), emotion (e.g., guilt or sorrow), and behavior (e.g., apology, confession, or restitution). They found that measures for developmental level of rea- soning about forgiveness, narcissism, and self-monitoring significantly predicted seeking forgiveness, but religiosity and age were not significant predictors. Gordon, Baucom et al. (2004) tested an empirical model of an intervention to promote recovery from extramarital affairs in six couples. Although the sample size was small, their model was effective and dem- onstrated how forgiveness was integrated within an overall intervention model specifically designed for the treatment of couples in which one partner had engaged in an extramarital affair. In contrast to other re- searchers, Aquino, Tripp, and Bies (2001) linked reconciliation to for- giveness when they defined reconciliation as a behavioral manifestation of forgiveness. Commentary Reconciling and Reconciliation An extensive commentary on reconciling and reconciliation would be premature because there have been so few studies. From a concep- tual perspective, we need to better understand the dimensions of recon- ciliation within interpersonal relationships and other small groups (e.g., family, work groups), as well as between large social groups. We also need to understand the boundaries of the construct relative to forgive- ness and restoration. As in our discussion of forgiveness, we propose that reconciliation and reconciling may be considered respectively as a state and a process. It is important to understand the dimensions of a rec- onciled relationship (state), as well as the dimensions of relationships in the process of reconciling. We need to consider what it means to be par- tially versus completely reconciled or even to experience a relationship that is enhanced because of the reconciling process. In consideration of the limited empirical data, we tentatively offer the following definitions of reconciliation (state) and reconciling (process). Reconciliation is a new state of closeness that exists between or among people who were separated because of a transgression committed by one or more of those persons. The state is characterized by prosocial behav- iors. Some of the people have likely experienced positive intrapersonal change in the forgiving process. Reconciling is a process of building a re- lationship between or among people following a transgression that Geoffrey W. Sutton and Eloise K. Thomas 35 caused a disruption. Reconciling includes various verbal and nonverbal behavior patterns that suggest no significant transgression will recur. RESTORING AND RESTORATION WITHIN A COMMUNITY Conceptualizations of Restoring and Restoration Within a Community Restoration has been discussed in association with reconciliation in the context of repairing trust damaged because of an interpersonal of- fense (McCullough & Worthington, 1994; Worthington & Drinkard, 2000; Worthington & Wade, 1999). In the context of the justice system, Worthington (2000) addressed forgiveness related to three parties and their supporters: a victim, an offender, and society. The justice system involves society in the process of forgiving when acts are taken to re- store offenders and victims to their respective communities. The con- cept of restorative justice was exemplified through programs in which offenders confessed and apologized to their victims or their representa- tives. Hughes and Armstrong (1995) differentiated between restoration within a religious community and restoration to pastoral leadership. In particular, they proposed that clergy who have committed adultery should not be re- stored to pastoral leadership. According to Wells (2003), 74% of respon- dents believed that sexually offending clergy should be allowed to return to ministry situations in which they have no access to victims. However, 44% said they should not be able to return to “active pastoral ministry” (p. 213). Sutton and Thomas (2005) used case narratives to examine the be- liefs of experienced pastors toward married male pastors who had been involved in an affair or a romantic relationship and were either young or middle-aged. They conceptualized restoration as a return to public min- istry, either in the position previously held or in another position that could include nonpublic ministry. Commentary on Restoring and Restoration Within a Community As with reconciliation, few researchers have conducted empirical stud- ies of restoration or developed definitions informed by research findings. The term restoration can serve as a metaconcept if one considers forgive- ness as part of a therapeutic restoration of a person who has been hurt and reconciliation as the restoration of two parties who have experienced a loss of relationship quality. However, when people are restored to their commu- nities, no one has to forgive them although forgiveness would likely pro- 36 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING mote restoration. Clearly, the restoration process may be analogous to the process of interpersonal reconciliation, yet it is possible for people to be re- stored to their communities without ever experiencing even a partial recon- ciliation with some members of the community albeit successful inter- personal reconciliations would likely promote restoration. Restoring a person to wholeness and restoring a person to community involve more than is accounted for by the concepts of forgiveness or reconciliation. Restoration includes a return to a position of status that was previously held. We recognize that status is a rather vague term, but we conceive of status as including the roles and respect a person had be- fore the transgression. The meaning of restoration is contextual. Each offender and each community will define the objectives to be accom- plished within the process of restoring and the criteria for a completed state of restoration. Presumably, both parties may concur that, after some process, the only mutually agreed upon outcome is some degree of partial restoration. At this point, we offer our definitions of restora- tion as a state of attainment and as a process that will lead to some de- gree of restoration. We have used the qualifier intracommunity because we wish to distinguish this concept of restoration from the way those writing about reconciliation (e.g., Worthington & Drinkard, 2000) have used restoration. Intracommunity restoration is a state that exists when community leaders affirm a status for an offender who lost such a status following a transgression. The status may or may not include all of the same features as the status held before the transgression but must be considered acceptable to the leaders and the offender to constitute resto- ration. A person’s status within a community often includes such fea- tures as employment, memberships, and participation in formal and informal gatherings. A partial restoration is a state that is perceived by the leader-offender and the community to be less than the leader’s status before the transgression. Full restoration is a state that is perceived by the leader-offender and the community to be the same or similar to the status the leader had before the transgression. Further, intracommunity restoring is a process whereby community leaders and an offender engage in certain behaviors deemed necessary by one or both parties for the offender to achieve a mutually agreeable status within a community following the loss of such a status. Restoring Leaders to Wholeness: Practice Applications At this point we return to our scenario of pastors who have been sepa- rated from their communities due to extramarital affairs with congre- Geoffrey W. Sutton and Eloise K. Thomas 37 gants. In the example presented, the victims would, at a minimum, include the pastor, spouse, children, affair partner, spouse, and children. In addition, we assume there will be a negative impact on various mem- bers of their congregations. In this context, we offer the following sug- gestions: 1. Use a wholistic model (e.g., SCOPES) to evaluate and treat the spiritual, psychological, and other needs of the leader and the direct impact victims. Crisis intervention comes first. Next, fo- cus attention on identifying stress disorder symptoms. Con- sider the possibility of using empirically supported treatments for PTSD. 2. Take a forgiveness history. Explore the potential for receiving and offering forgiveness. Evaluate the strength of a disposition to forgive. 3. If reconciliation is a desirable and safe goal between various pairs of individuals, consider employing the model presented by Gordon, Baucom et al. (2004), which has some empirical support and in- cludes a forgiveness component. 4. Educate community members about forgiveness, including the distinction between forgiveness, reconciliation, and restoration. Expectations about the forgiveness response in others may be un- realistic if the leader believes forgiveness and reconciliation occur together. Leaders may assume they have been forgiven if they ex- perience prosocial behaviors suggesting a desire to reconcile. They may assume reconciliation has occurred if they seek and re- ceive forgiveness. They may assume they are on the way to resto- ration to the community if they perceive either forgiveness has been granted or reconciliation has occurred with one or more per- sons. Victims who believe forgiveness requires reconciliation may be revictimized (Fincham & Kashdan, in press). Victims may feel a sense of empowerment when they realize they can forgive without reconciling. In addition, they can forgive and speak for or against a part of a restoration plan for reasons of justice or concern about safety issues. The public education ideas of Fincham and Kashdan (in press) appear valuable here. 5. Educate people about restoration to community status as a sepa- rate albeit related concept. Explain that there is no defined restora- tion process that will lead to a specific outcome. Explain that restoration is a matter of perspective, and seek to clarify the per- spectives of the involved parties. 38 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING 6. Educate community members about research related to forgive- ness. For example: a. Note that forgiveness out of obligation rather than love may not result in beneficial health effects (Huang & Enright, 2000). b. Consider that women under moral pressure to forgive may be under pressure to reconcile as well (Gordon, Baucom et al., 2004). c. Forgiveness appears to be associated with positive mental health outcomes (e.g., Touissant, Williams, Musick, & Everson, 2001; Wuthnow, 2000). d. Self-forgiveness can have beneficial physical and mental health results. e. The capacity to seek and grant forgiveness is a key to a long and satisfactory marriage (Fennell, 1993). 7. Evaluate ways, other than forgiveness, that the people may be us- ing to cope with the transgression event. 8. Select measures to suit your definition and documentation of progress. Presumably, it would be good to know how clients have responded to the transgression situation (current point in the pro- cess), whether they attained a state of forgiveness toward a past offender (state conceptualization), and whether they are generally disposed to forgive people (personality trait). 9. Consider viewing the problem of spouses remaining in abusive re- lationships from the perspective of social exchange theory. In ad- dition, forgiveness has been shown to explain part of a woman’s sense of commitment in abusive relationships (Gordon, Burton, & Porter, 2004). Although research does not address abusive rela- tionships in which a man is the victim, clinicians may evaluate whether or not the findings for women apply to men as well. 10. Consider expanding the components of the Gordon, Baucom et al. (2004) model to treat extramarital affairs in couples within a com- munity setting. Presumably, many members of the community may experience a similar recovery process albeit at a lesser level of intensity than those members who were closely involved with the leader and the transgression. When recovering alcoholics in AA fail to complete the 4th Step inventory, then the power of resent- ment knows no limitations. This lack of action on the part of the AA member by failing to participate in Step 4 only prolongs emotional pain, delays recovery, and deepens the effects of alcoholism–a process which is deadly both emotionally and mentally. 44 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING One is reminded of the analogy the Killer Bees that have invaded southern portions of the United States. The stings of these bees inject a poison that is so toxic that an accumulation of multiple stings within a short period of time potentially could kill a person. Mind-Acid, Soul Corrosive In examining the effects of an accumulation of resentful thoughts let us now consider the effect upon the body. Imagine a stainless steel 55-gallon drum. Suppose that each day an automobile mechanic were to pour out the liquid contents of a battery into that steel drum. He might pour up to a half quart of a strong acid into that empty steel container. Day after day the mechanic sees the level of the acid rising slowly. One day, perhaps after a few weeks, the acid would find a weak spot in the container and slowly eat its way through. Initially, the acid would slowly trickle. Later, the acid would pour out of the metal barrel spew- ing out the corrosive contents onto the ground. The degree of acidity of the soil would prohibit the growth of any vegetation in the area. The sur- face of the ground within close proximity to the damaged barrel would resemble a wasteland. Unfortunately, most alcoholics are so full of resentment that they are not able to see the effects that this mind-acid, or soul corrosive has upon them. The emotions associated with the resentment process resemble a bleak wasteland. But awareness of this process does not stop the pro- gression and deterioration. In fact, some alcoholics actively relish the emotional and physical sensations associated with anger and rage. Some take delight in the physically burning sensation that the emotion of anger evokes within the viscera. Surely, an injection of thimbleful of a mild acid into one’s circulatory system would produce a similar burn- ing sensation, but the physical damage could be irreversible. Actively drinking alcoholics often review a series of resentments on a daily basis. A similar process can be seen in Shakespeare’s MacBeth (Act 3 Scene 2) as MacBeth tells his wife “O full of scorpions is my mind.” This pattern adequately describes the alcoholic’s thinking hab- its. In fact, alcoholics often use resentments to excuse themselves for all of their wrongful actions and then transfer the blame onto someone else. This routine is likely to be the main reason why alcoholics choose to stay in resentment. Jeff Sandoz 45 Each time the alcoholic replays the hurtful event he/she looks more and more innocent and the other person appears to be more malicious and cruel. Resentful alcoholics view themselves as hurt victims and they must view themselves in this manner otherwise the emotional pain would be unbearable. Resentment’s Purpose The purpose and function of a resentment is four-fold: 1. To avoid responsibility of looking at oneself critically and honestly with the hope of escaping from the possibility of having done some- thing wrong. 2. To escape by shifting the blame onto someone else, 3. To declare that the blamed person has hurt us, and finally 4. To withdraw in justification of the next drinking episode by claim- ing that the person blamed drove the alcoholic to drink. Therefore, the reason that alcoholics cling to resentments is because they convince themselves into the belief that they are not responsible for any possible wrongdoing. Denton, DMin The four of them sat around the red chrome kitchen table so familiar to those of us who grew up in the 1950s. One was an Iwo Jima Marine who had already been bloodied by combat when he climbed down Ja- cob’s Ladder into the Higgins Boat bound for what he knew then only as ‘X-Ray Island.’ Another was one of the ‘Emperor’s Girls’ who had grown up on the island of Hokkaido and pledged to kill ten Marines when they invaded her homeland.1 A third was a retired Army nurse who had been a guest of the Japanese Army as it ‘escorted’ prisoners away from the island of Bataan; she had also been a guest of one of Mao Tse-tung’s interrogators as his Red Army swept its way across China. Finally there was another Marine who had spent her time cooking for Marines deploying into the Pacific’s unrelenting hell. My parents were the two Marines. The two other women were nurses and friends of my Mother’s from her work. By the time these nighttime conversations took place I was entering adolescence. This afforded me enough knowledge to understand the content of their mutual storytell- ing and enough wisdom to remain silent unless directly asked a ques- tion. My job was to make sure the coffee cups stayed full and my younger brother entertained, “So that your Mother doesn’t have to do all the work around here,” as my Father nicely put it. All rights reserved. doi:10.1300/J062v08n02_05 73 I believe the first task of being an effective counselor is ‘knowing when you’ve struck gold in the conversation,’ as my first supervisor said. Listening to these four people work their way through horrible memories with humor, grit, and hospitality tuned my ear to recognize the gold in the conversation. Watching my Father’s growing protective- ness toward Judy Bishop was an early lesson in the timeline and possi- bilities of forgiveness; hearing Miss Crim play the violin which she had carried in the prison camps with her now-crippled fingers alerted me to the cleansing power of music; moving my Mother away from the sink and onto her kitchen stool helped me learn the significance of where people sat when the conversation turned serious. Theoreticians like Minuchin and Yalom, Gerkin and Pruyser later sup- plied me with names and strategies for the healing process. But my ear was tuned toward the therapeutic process around that red kitchen table. It is a process I repeated around another Table years later as I gathered vet- erans from my own war in the sanctuaries of Richmond churches to flesh out the basic insight expressed by Vicktor Frankl: “A man who becomes conscious of the responsibility he bears toward a human being who affec- tionately waits for him, or to an unfinished work, will never be able to throw away his life. He knows the ‘why’ for his existence, and will be able to bear almost any ‘how.’2 In addition to those early overheard con- versations and my own discovery of the responsibility I bear to the unfin- ished work of soothing wounded souls, I have benefited from scholars and supervisors who provided me with maps for that wilderness and skills to sustain people as they walk toward the high ground and sunny places of health. Among all of the scholars and supervisors who taught me to recog- nize the various grounds of being upon which the therapeutic conversa- tion might be held, no one stands higher for me or embodies more of how to conduct the art of pastoral counseling than James Ashbrook. “We’re really not sure how your brain works,” he said aloud with his hallmark gentle laugh as I wrote ambidextrously on the blackboard. James Ashbrook embodied the mind of a research-oriented scholar, the insight of a wise advisor and the courage of a lion. He encouraged my writing for professional journals and insisted that my doctoral re- search project meet rigorous statistical standards. His method of using objects to facilitate both instruction and healing still resonates in my own supervision and therapeutic work. His capacity to find meaning in the face of his cancer by remaining an active educator is the signature of courage. 74 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING “Have him bring along something that is important to him,” I typi- cally tell parents of the young men who find their way toward my office. “Anything?!” their mother’s usually ask. “Just as long as it fits in the car and won’t make a mess in my office,” I respond. Much thanks to James Ashbrook, there have been hamsters and Barbie Dolls, electric guitars and totems from the pit of the Grand Canyon accompanying these youngsters as they struggle to find a way to be special within a family trying to hang on to them or a community intent on discarding them. Ashbrook’s use of objects for theological reflection was not merely a cutesy way of getting to know a new client. It’s most powerful applica- tion occurred within group supervision where another person unfamil- iar with the content of the case about to be presented offers the object for theological reflection at the beginning of the group’s process. This application deepens the clinical insight into the case under consider- ation and underscores something inherent in his brain research: the inter-connective capacity of the brain’s right hemisphere to leap across time and space in such a way that one was always able to ‘know more than you can say’ about any situation if one takes the time to be attentive to the right brain’s images. For James Ashbrook this is a phenomena rich with theological implications; an insight that has profound impli- cations for the care of souls. The use of objects and an active awareness of the right brain’s capac- ity to lead both client and clinician to the meaning inherent in disparate images, playful impulses and unspeakable terror addresses the funda- mental human struggle that finds the meaning inherent in profound suf- fering that was identified by Frankl and given voice most eloquently by Job: “Therefore I have uttered what I did not understand, things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.”3 In my work with adults this has led me to the clinical use of the expressive arts and guiding them into a discovery of the Classics in addition to the measured use of tradi- tional spiritual disciplines such as prayer, meditation and reflection on Scripture. In my work with children it has reinforced my use of play therapy and the use of Gardener’s technique of mutual storytelling be- cause Ashbrook’s insight into the functioning of the brain underscores the inherently eternal seriousness of these seemingly simple avenues to healing. Having had my own baptism of fire in Vietnam that reinforced my earliest exposure to humanity’s fundamental brokenness, I found James Ashbrook’s optimism about the healing potential inherent in the human brain to be balanced by his awareness of how we nevertheless “fail to understand each other.” He saw in the brain the roots of how “differenti- The Greatest Influence on My Pastoral Counseling 75 ation contributes opposition. Dichotomies become dualities. Polar con- trasts result in polarizations. Human minds turn against themselves, one another, and God.”4 More recent research has highlighted this duality as rising not merely because of the brain’s two hemispheres but in the rela- tionship between the mid-brain region (where our survival impulses re- side) and our frontal lobe (where our moral reasoning resides). Ash- brook’s research prompted me to look widely for tools through which both of these regions could be healed: words and linear experiences that would restore rational sanity to the left brain’s frontal lobe and mid-brain region as well as images and experiences of Pentecost that would restore relational sanity to the right brain’s frontal lobe and mid-brain region. Put another way, I wondered ‘what experiences can be provided within the traditional 50 minute hour of outpatient pastoral counseling that will expose the client’s brain to the deep-structure that Ashbrook contends is divine?’5 I have certainly benefited from deploying the magic question of Scott Miller’s Solution Focused Therapy with Ashbrook’s under- standing in mind. But what does brain research offer as therapeutic tools if a person’s fundamental ability to solve problems is impaired by chronic drug use or a couple’s hostility is fueled by massive be- trayal or contempt? Ashbrook’s research pointed me in the direction of communities: “I contend that the deep structure of humanity bears thetrueimage of divinity...weonly access deep community through surface communities.”6 As a consequence, I utilize the resources of several surface communi- ties in my work as a pastoral counselor–resources utilized not merely because they are handy and helpful but because their helpfulness is rooted in their capacity to provide hurting people an encounter with deep structure. These surface communities include, but are not limited to, the great resources of religious faith, the practical assets of the Twelve Step movement, the moral formation and leadership training of the Scouting movements and the well-timed use of a game of chess with a child struggling to learn how to sit still and think through the conse- quences of an action before he takes it. This latter activity, frequently taking place after a leisurely stroll around the office complex grounds near my office, provides the yet-forming brain of a child with a life-en- hancing totality that includes motion, sound, scent, touch as well as words. Having practiced pastoral counseling in a single community now for twenty years, the witness of people to the effectiveness of these tools comes from former clients who come up to me and say things like this: 76 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PASTORAL COUNSELING ‘I can still hear your voice urging me to do the next right thing’ or ‘when you suggested I get involved with the Ronald McDonald House, I thought they wouldn’t want me–boy was I wrong’ or ‘when I walked in here and saw that well-worn Bible, I knew that whatever other training you had, you were on speaking terms with the Great Physician.’ These sentiments are not unique to me; rather, they simply illustrate this truth–while we do not know what word or image will prove to be the le- ver that unleashes the river of healing in the brain, an effective therapist must deploy themselves and the space around them with an eye and ear turned toward intentionally influencing the brain’s deep structures. This takes me well beyond the well-known Rogerian style so popular in my earliest training programs and points toward the research on brain intunement.7 I want to say a bit, finally about the way I frame the task of diagnosis as naming the pain and guiding the care. I believe I am the one who coined this phrase although I stand ready to be corrected by a colleague with a better memory than Google. My clients have been the ones who have influenced me in arriving at this formulation. They know they are hurting; otherwise they would not be in my office–so I recognized early they are not shy about having some nomenclature attached to their con- dition. More importantly, they desire to be well and want to know if I can be helpful and how I intend to help them–so I needed to find a way of framing the therapeutic task in a manner that is distinctive for a counseling pastor. Some pain comes from the consequences of ‘doing what I should not do and leaving undone what I should have done.’ I have found most people coming for outpatient counseling are willing to acknowledge this aspect of their situation once they realize they will not be further shamed by the counselor–and that the counselor is capable of helping them make some type of amend and work to inoculate them against additional ethical lapses. Some other pain comes from the result of “taking a limited expres- sion of reality as the whole of reality.”8 What secular clinicians and the DSM-IV may call a personality disorder or character disorder, religious counselors and theologians recognize as idolatry. This is serious pain that wages war as readily against the soul of a culture as against the con- duct of a single person crying among the tombs.9 While as clinicians we may be hesitant to name this pain in a document that will haunt the indi- vidual’s life, cringing at honestly naming this level of human bondage is singularly unhelpful if not unethical. The Greatest Influence on My Pastoral Counseling 77 Finally there is a quality of pain that is the result of some massive cat- astrophic insult to the person. Sometimes the individual is left visibly altered or obviously impaired but more frequently this pain exists be- yond the left-brain’s capacity for articulation and the human soul must marshal all of its resources to rebuild life upon a foundation that appears to have been utterly shattered. I have found people regularly turn to reli- gious language or imagery to express this epic journey. These resources affirm to the one who suffers that their suffering is both a struggle and a gift. Regardless of what resources help them name this pain, it is imper- ative they understand the rest of their life will be organized in a large part around the task of caring for this stain. In those conversations around that red kitchen table there were mo- ments when it got strangely quiet. Only after beginning to face my own brokenness did I gain some insight into the nature and importance of such silence. It is the humble awareness that one stands in the presence of Mystery, a Mystery that while pulsing beyond our words and under- standing nevertheless understands us thoroughly and remembers that we are made from dust. Without a doubt this Mystery has utilized all these instruments to shape my life and my work. Selah! NOTES 1. Coulter I met Robert Perske in the fall of 1965 while participating in an Intro- ductory to Clinical Pastoral Education course while a student at Saint Paul School of Theology in Kansas City, Missouri. I was struck by two observations during our brief time together. The first was his excitement about ministry with children and youth whose lives were complexed by their mental retardation. My second observation was his ability to explore the realm of worship through the use of the senses of his parishioners. His willingness to resource their experience, to draw forth their strengths and needs, and to take seriously their lives was an inspiration. Bob Perske’s writings span the years from 1965 to 1971. They provide a developmental perspective to his experience with and understanding of ministry with this unique community. His writings also reflect a transi- tion of understanding in the broader field of mental retardation. A unique aspect of Bob Perske’s work is the view of the developmen- tally disabled as part of the larger community rather than a community set off, separated from the world. Nothing displays this view better than in the piece entitled, “New Approaches to Religious Education Programs Book Reviews 81 for the Mentally Retarded.” He recounts the story of a boy who put to- gether his excitement in singing with the caroling done for the Kansas Neurological Institute population by youth groups from area churches. It washis affirmationthat“...wecan sing betterthantheycan!” that evolved into the group caroling to nursing homes. This evolved into the youth taking on several nursing homes to continue “their ministry” to the el- derly, to other youth beyond the institution, and to “their sick comrades ...” Who could imagine the “cared for community” becoming a community that actively sought out and provided ministry to others. Perske believes in ministry as a manifestation of continuing creation. He involves the reader in the active process of doing theology and sup- ports a belief in the ability of clergy to use our own sensitivity to per- son’s needs, our experience and skill at writing appropriate curriculum for use with the developmentally disabled. He carries us through some of his own process in the development of the same for his work at Kan- sas Neurological Institute. In the process he evolves a theology to de- velop, support and maintain this ministry. His writings on “The Chaplain’s Role in an Institution for the Mentally Retarded” and “An Attempt to Find an Adequate Theological View of Mental Retardation” should be required reading for anyone pursuing a graduate degree in Ministry and will be required reading for my Pastoral Counseling Stu- dents. His penchant for doing theology as an outgrowth of his own en- counter with the suffering and repression of persons is a model of ministry to be repeated. It is a hopeful sign that the voice of God is con- tinuing in the presence of all creation. It is the encounter with continu- ing creation in the presence of the mentally retarded and the response of persons both among and working with developmentally disabled per- sons that marks Perske’s work as both a gift and a model to be pursued. In reading the evolution of his ministry we become involved with both the problems and the solutions as they evolve out of a creative commu- nity that society more commonly over looks. His model of looking at the developmentally disabled in terms of abilities and needs certainly presents a different perspective on ministry. It is the task of doing with rather than doing for, that is the cutting edge in his work. The Pastoral Voice of Robert Perske is a resource in the task of ministry, one that actively engages our own person in the task. It is a significant re- source for clergy in this time of searching out and resourcing how we do ministry and how we do worship in the context of community. Reviewed by Roger Q. Harmon Roger Q.
